documents.title: batch_server program description
documents.text:
Title: batch_server program description
Domain: workload

# What the `batch_server` program does

This document describes the `batch_server` program: what it is, what its threads do, and what
its activity looks like in an LTTng kernel trace.

## Summary

`batch_server` is a multi-threaded **batch-processing server** running on Linux for a fixed length
of time (2, 10 or 30 minutes). The program runs in repeated **rounds**, about 11 per second. In
each round:

1. A coordinator thread hands one batch of work to each of 4 worker threads and waits for all of
   them to finish.
2. Each worker does a short burst of computation.
3. One worker also commits its results to a shared in-memory cache that is protected by a lock.
4. A background `flusher` thread writes the cache back to storage. In the program this write is
   simulated with a sleep while holding the cache lock.

When every worker has finished, the round ends. The coordinator then idles for 50 ms and starts
the next round. All of the program's threads run on a single CPU (CPU 3).

## Threads

The names are the `comm` / thread names you see in the trace.

| Thread | Count | Role | Activity per round |
|---|---|---|---|
| `batch_server` | 1 | Coordinator (main thread, PID = its TID) | Starts the round, wakes the flusher and all workers, blocks until the last worker reports done, then sleeps 50 ms |
| `worker-0`, `worker-1`, `worker-3` | 3 | Compute workers | Wait for a batch, spin on the CPU for about 5 ms, report done |
| `worker-2` | 1 | Compute worker that also owns the commit step | Waits for a batch, spins about 5 ms, takes `cache_lock`, commits the round's results, releases the lock, reports done |
| `flusher` | 1 | Background cache write-back | Waits to be told to flush, takes `cache_lock`, writes back the previous batch (a 40 ms sleep standing in for disk I/O), releases the lock |

## Lifecycle of one run

1. **Startup** (well under a second)
   - The process starts and pins itself to CPU 3; all threads it creates inherit this.
   - It calibrates a CPU busy-loop (about 50–100 ms of pure computation on the main thread).
   - It creates 4 workers and 1 flusher (`clone3`, thread stacks via `mmap`), then waits 100 ms.
   - It prints its PID and thread IDs to stdout.
2. **Steady state** (the requested duration). Rounds repeat as described above.
   - Expected round counts: about 1,300 for 2 minutes, about 6,600 for 10 minutes, about 19,800
     for 30 minutes.
   - All round bookkeeping goes to memory allocated up front, so this phase makes no file I/O,
     network, `brk` or `mmap` calls.
3. **Shutdown**
   - The coordinator tells every thread to exit and joins them.
   - It writes two result files to disk, a JSON summary and a CSV of per-round timings (`mkdir`,
     `openat`, `write`, `close`).
   - It prints a short summary and exits.

## What this looks like in the kernel trace

**Scheduling events.** `sched_switch` / `sched_wakeup` between the 6 threads, all on CPU 3, in a
regular pattern every ~90 ms:
- The coordinator wakes, wakes the flusher and the workers, then blocks.
- Workers run one after another on the shared CPU.
- The coordinator is woken at the end of the round, then sleeps.

**System calls:**
- `futex` (wait/wake) from the semaphores that start and finish each round, and from `cache_lock`
  when it is contended.
- `clock_nanosleep` from the coordinator's 50 ms gap and the flusher's simulated write-back.
- Almost nothing else during the steady state. The CPU work is a pure computation loop with no
  system calls, so it appears only as time in the RUNNING state.

**Timer / interrupt events.** hrtimer expiries waking the sleeping threads.

**Other processes.** The trace is system-wide, so it also contains everything else on the machine
(desktop, daemons, the LTTng session daemon, kernel threads). `batch_server` and its threads are
the workload under study.

## What the program does *not* do

- No network activity (no sockets).
- No real disk I/O during the steady state. The "write-back" is a sleep, so there are no
  block-device requests from this program until it writes its two result files at exit.
- No child processes (`fork`/`exec`). Only threads.
- No reading of input files.

documents.title: Limits of kernel-only evidence
documents.text:
Title: Limits of kernel-only evidence
Domain: trace_compass

# Limits of kernel-only evidence

Kernel traces are strong evidence for scheduling states, syscalls, interrupts,
CPU activity, and some resource interactions. They are weaker evidence for
application-level ownership unless identifiers are correlated.

A kernel socket wait proves a socket wait. It does not automatically prove
which Django request, database query, cache call, HTTP client, or remote
service caused the wait.

LTTng Kernel Analysis

Historically, LTTng was developed to trace the Linux kernel and, over time, a number of kernel-oriented analysis views were developed and organized in a perspective.

This section presents a description of the 
 OS Tracing Overview perspective and the 
 LTTng Kernel perspective.

OS Tracing Overview Perspective

The 
 OS Tracing Overview perspective groups the following views:

 Project Explorer View

 Events Editor

 Histogram View

 CPU Usage View

 Disk I/O Activity View

 Kernel Memory Usage View

The perspective can be opened from the Eclipse Open Perspective dialog (
 Window > Open Perspective... > Other).

This perspective is intended to be used to locate performance issues by observing resource usage.

The perspective can show times resource usage is anomalous. This can help locating the causes of system slowdowns in throughput or response time.

An example can be program that is doing a lot of processing then slows down due to a database access. The user will see a dip in CPU usage and maybe a slight rise in I/O access. The user should consider both spike and slums to be an indication of an area worth investigating.

Once a performance issue has been localized, it can be further investigated with the #LTTng kernel Perspective.

documents.title: Cross-Host TCP Message Matching
documents.text:
Title: Cross-Host TCP Message Matching
Domain: trace_compass

# Cross-Host TCP Message Matching

To synchronize traces from different machines, and to understand causal
relationships between hosts, Trace Compass can match TCP packets sent from
one traced host to their corresponding arrival on another traced host. Only
TCP packets can be matched this way. A match is made by comparing each
packet's sequence number, acknowledgement number, and TCP flags between a
send-side event on one trace and a receive-side event on another -- the
same identifying fields a TCP stack itself uses to track a segment.

One supported method for capturing the data this matching needs is the
"addons" kernel module, which adds dynamic instrumentation on TCP packets.
It captures events such as `inet_sock_local_out` (a packet leaving a
socket) and `inet_sock_local_in` (a packet arriving at a socket), each
carrying the sequence number, acknowledgement number, and flags needed for
matching, along with the source and destination address/port. Only TCP
packets are captured by this method; other protocols are not matched.

Once a send event on one host's trace is matched to its corresponding
receive event on another host's trace, the interval between them is real
evidence of a message having crossed between those two specific hosts, and
of how long that transit took. This is a different kind of evidence than a
single host's own syscall trace: a `sendto` or `recvfrom` syscall only
proves that a socket operation happened locally, not which other traced
host, if any, the data actually reached or came from. Matching closes that
gap for TCP traffic specifically, when both ends of the connection were
captured in the same combined experiment.

A message that cannot be matched is not proof that no data was
exchanged -- it may mean the peer was not being traced, the traffic used a
different protocol than TCP, or the matching data was not present in this
particular capture.

Trace Compass User Guide - Trace synchronization

 Trace synchronization

 LTTng-UST Analyses

 Time offsetting

Trace synchronization

It is possible to synchronize traces from different machines so that they have the same time reference. Events from the reference trace will have the same timestamps as usual, but the events from traces synchronized with the first one will have their timestamps transformed according to the formula obtained after synchronization.

Obtain synchronizable traces

To synchronize traces from different machines, they need to exchange packets through the network and have events enabled such that the data can be matched from one trace to the other. For now, only TCP packets can be matched between two traces.

LTTng traces that can be synchronized are obtained using one of three methods below. All methods are compatible so a trace on one host taken with one method can be synchronized with a trace on another host taken with another method:

Use LTTng-modules 2.9+

As of LTTng-modules 2.9, the 
 net_dev_queue and 
 net_if_receive_skb tracepoints contain all the necessary data to synchronize the traces.

LTTng-module network tracepoint with complete data

The tracepoints 
 net_dev_queue and 
 netif_receive_skb will be used for synchronization. Both tracepoints are available in lttng-modules since version 2.2, but they do not contain sufficient data to be used to synchronize traces.

documents.title: Critical Path (Process Wait Analysis)
documents.text:
Title: Critical Path (Process Wait Analysis)
Domain: trace_compass

# Critical Path (Process Wait Analysis)

Trace Compass can recover the wait causes of local and distributed processes
using operating system events. The analysis highlights the tasks and devices
causing a process to wait, by following the chain of scheduling and wake-up
events backward through however many other threads -- and, when traces from
multiple machines are combined with clock synchronization, however many other
hosts -- are causally involved.

This is a different question than "what does the Control Flow view show for
this one thread." A single thread's BLOCKED/RUNNING breakdown only describes
that thread's own states; it does not say why another thread's actions
determined how long those waits lasted. The critical path instead answers
"which other threads' work is actually on the causal chain that explains this
thread's total duration" -- the same duration can be dominated by one other
thread doing real work, or by several threads and hosts handing dependencies
back and forth (a classic case for a distributed web application, where a
client's wait may be explained by work done by an application server and a
database server on two different machines).

The corresponding view in the UI is the Critical Flow View: right-clicking a
process in the Control Flow view and selecting "Follow" runs this analysis
and displays the result there, with vertical arrows representing
synchronization and communication between the processes involved.

The critical path is recursive and can span every task running on the
system, so a wide critical path is not itself evidence of a problem -- it
means many threads/hosts happened to be part of the causal chain, not that
all of them are the bottleneck. Identifying which specific participant
dominates the path's total duration still requires looking at how much of
that duration each participant's own segments account for.

documents.title: System calls as kernel boundary evidence
documents.text:
Title: System calls as kernel boundary evidence
Domain: kernel_tracing

# System calls as kernel boundary evidence

System calls are the interface between user-space code and the Linux kernel.
Tracing syscall entry and exit can show when a thread entered the kernel, how
long it stayed there, and which syscall name was involved.

The syscall name is strong evidence for the category of wait, but it is often
not enough to identify the application-level root cause. Pair syscall spans
with scheduling states and resource identifiers.
